title: Diagonal reduction for matrices with division on both sides
statement: Let $R$ be an associative ring with identity, not necessarily commutative, and let $\delta:R\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbf N$ be a function. Assume that for all $a,b\in R$ with $b\ne0$ there are $q,r,q',r'\in R$ such that $a=qb+r=bq'+r'$, with $r=0$ or $\delta(r)<\delta(b)$ and $r'=0$ or $\delta(r')<\delta(b)$. For every $m,n\geq0$ and every $m\times n$ matrix $C$ over $R$ [def-weil-matrix], there are invertible matrices $U\in\operatorname{Mat}_m(R)$ and $V\in\operatorname{Mat}_n(R)$ and elements $d_1,\ldots,d_{\min(m,n)}\in R$ such that $$ (UCV)_{ij}=\begin{cases}d_i&i=j,\\0&i\ne j.\end{cases} $$ Invertible means possessing a two-sided multiplicative inverse, and matrix multiplication is $(BC)_{ij}=\sum_k B_{ik}C_{kj}$. No divisibility relation among the $d_i$ is asserted. Empty matrices are allowed.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, printed p.297, the omitted matrix-reduction argument in the comparison with the polynomial-ring proof; supporting agent lemma (Berrick and Keating 2000, Theorem 3.3.6, cited there, is not available locally).

proof.text: For distinct indices $i,j$, let $e_{ij}(s)$ have entry $s$ at $(i,j)$ and zero elsewhere. Expanding the finite sums defining multiplication gives $e_{ij}(s)e_{ij}(t)=0$, so $(I+e_{ij}(s))(I-e_{ij}(s))=(I-e_{ij}(s))(I+e_{ij}(s))=I$. Left multiplication by $I+e_{ij}(s)$ replaces row $i$ by row $i+s\,\text{row }j$; right multiplication replaces column $j$ by column $j+(\text{column }i)s$. A row or column interchange is multiplication by its permutation matrix, whose inverse is the inverse permutation matrix. The same finite-sum expansion gives associativity, hence a product of such invertible matrices has inverse the reverse product of their inverses. These are direct calculations with the matrices of [def-weil-matrix], valid over an associative ring without commuting any coefficients.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, printed p.297 (PDF p.309), with the two division algorithms on printed p.296; agent supplies the omitted matrix argument, not the unavailable Berrick–Keating proof.

proof.text: Use strong induction on $k=\min(m,n)$, simultaneously for every matrix of each size with that value of $k$. If $k=0$, take $U=I_m,V=I_n$ and the empty list: there are no entries. At any size the zero matrix is already of the required form, with every $d_i=0$. Thus assume $m,n>0$ and $C\ne0$.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, printed p.297 (PDF p.309), with the two division algorithms on printed p.296; agent supplies the omitted matrix argument, not the unavailable Berrick–Keating proof.

proof.text: Among the nonzero entries of all matrices $PCQ$, where $P$ and $Q$ have two-sided inverses, choose an entry $d$ with least $\delta(d)$. This choice uses only a least natural number: a nonzero entry $c$ of $C=I_mCI_n$ gives an upper bound $\delta(c)$, so scan the finite list $0,\ldots,\delta(c)$ for the first value attained by a nonzero entry of an equivalent matrix. Choose a witnessing matrix and interchange rows and columns to obtain $A=PCQ$ with $A_{11}=d$. Minimality still concerns every nonzero entry of every matrix equivalent to $C$, not merely the entries of $A$.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, printed p.297 (PDF p.309), with the two division algorithms on printed p.296; agent supplies the omitted matrix argument, not the unavailable Berrick–Keating proof.

proof.text: For each $i>1$ use the assumed division $A_{i1}=q_i d+r_i$, where $r_i=0$ or $\delta(r_i)<\delta(d)$. Subtracting $q_i$ times row $1$ on the left from row $i$ is invertible by step 1 and puts $r_i$ in position $(i,1)$. A nonzero $r_i$ contradicts the minimum chosen in step 3; therefore $r_i=0$. Perform these operations for all $i>1$. Each leaves row $1$ and all other rows unchanged. Their product $L$ gives $B=LA$ with $B_{11}=d$ and $B_{i1}=0$ for $i>1$. Since $L$ is invertible, the same global minimum applies to every matrix equivalent to $B$.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, printed p.297 (PDF p.309), with the two division algorithms on printed p.296; agent supplies the omitted matrix argument, not the unavailable Berrick–Keating proof.

proof.text: For each $j>1$ use the other assumed division $B_{1j}=d q'_j+r'_j$, with $r'_j=0$ or $\delta(r'_j)<\delta(d)$. Replace column $j$ by column $j-(\text{column }1)q'_j$, using right multiplication by $I-e_{1j}(q'_j)$. It is invertible and makes its $(1,j)$ entry $r'_j$, so minimality forces $r'_j=0$. These operations leave column $1$ unchanged and, since $B_{i1}=0$ for $i>1$, leave every lower-right entry unchanged. Their product $T$ therefore satisfies $LPCQT=\begin{pmatrix}d&0\\0&H\end{pmatrix}$, with $H$ of size $(m-1)\times(n-1)$. No assertion about divisibility of entries of $H$ is needed.

source.place: Proposition 14.51, printed p.297 (PDF p.309), with the two division algorithms on printed p.296; agent supplies the omitted matrix argument, not the unavailable Berrick–Keating proof.

proof.text: Now $\min(m-1,n-1)=k-1$. The induction hypothesis gives invertible $U_0,V_0$ with $U_0HV_0$ rectangular diagonal. Put $\widehat U=\operatorname{diag}(1,U_0)$ and $\widehat V=\operatorname{diag}(1,V_0)$. Their two-sided inverses are $\operatorname{diag}(1,U_0^{-1})$ and $\operatorname{diag}(1,V_0^{-1})$, by direct block multiplication. Thus $U=\widehat ULP$ and $V=QT\widehat V$ are invertible and $UCV=\begin{pmatrix}d&0\\0&U_0HV_0\end{pmatrix}$. Its off-diagonal entries vanish and its diagonal list is $d$ followed by the $k-1$ entries supplied by induction. This completes the induction, including the cases $m=1$ or $n=1$, when $H$ has an empty dimension.
